body.text: As the Fiji Airways flight carrying dignitaries to Tuvalu sat on the airport runway at the heart of its tiny capital, Funafuti, an official struggled with a broken umbrella in the driving rain.

A pile of sodden brollies lay next to him as locals prepared to ferry leaders, ministers and assorted bigwigs out of the plane, across the tarmac, through the downpour, and into a traditional welcome ceremony.

The rather forlorn image seemed to fit neatly with the headlines back home in Australia, which had already declared the pre-COP summit a farce and a failure, particularly as the government had only managed to coax two non-Pacific leaders to fly to Tuvalu to see the climate emergency up close.
On the face of it, this might seem a little unfair.
By all accounts, the vibe on the ground was not nearly so grim.
After all, Tuvalu — which remains one of the most isolated and hard to reach countries in the world — is hardly famous for hosting major diplomatic gatherings.
And yet here they all were.
Pacific leaders standing side by side with ministers from across the world, including from India, the United Arab Emirates, Türkiye and Nepal.

UN heavyweights and top multilateral officials who hold the keys to billions in climate financing. All listening in person to Tuvalu's story, and examining an extraordinary land reclamation project designed to hold back relentless rising seas.
The carping and outrage about the cost to Australian taxpayers was also, frankly, a bit over the top.

When the cameras caught Climate Minister Chris Bowen apparently struggling to resist nodding off, the Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan joked he was having a rest after a "big day … by the pool on the banana lounge sipping a few cocktails".
But anyone who has had even a passing interaction with the famously diligent minister would laugh-choke into their piña colada at the implausible image of Mr Bowen gleefully dodging work by the pool.
And while it is always good to scrutinise government spending, let's keep some perspective.
The rough cost of the whole enterprise of around $20 million (or so) is somewhere between loose change and a minor rounding error.
It would buy about one seventh of a single F-35 fighter jet, or fund the NDIS for approximately three hours.
So, does all this mean that pre-COP was a great success, and that the carping critics have got it wrong?
Nope.
Because even when you cast aside the exaggeration and cheap shots, there is still simply no way for the federal government to hide the yawning gap between what it promised, and what it has delivered.
'We wanted to bring the world to Tuvalu'

When the government struck its rather ungainly bargain with Türkiye, it spruiked the pre-COP meetings in Tuvalu and Fiji as a spur to global climate action, bringing the world's polluters to the Pacific to see the devastating impact of the catastrophe in person.
COP could not just be a "jamboree of the willing" Mr Bowen told the Guardian in January.

Anthony Albanese has rapidly built up a fairly impressive network among fellow world leaders, and government officials were not shy about spruiking his "exceptional" personal relationships across Asia and Europe, suggesting that the prime minister might be able to land some big fish for Tuvalu.

Sure, there was zero chance of bringing in an apex predator like Donald Trump or Xi Jinping, but hopes seemed high that some heavyweights — like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, or then UK prime minister Keir Starmer — might be coaxed into making the trip.

But as the months dragged on, and leader after leader quietly let it be known they would not be willing to make a long journey to the Pacific, the mood shifted, accompanied by the groaning sound of goalposts being dragged across the ground.
Ministers were allowed to sub in for leaders.
About a month ago Fiji revealed that a grand total of just five leaders from outside the Pacific had agreed to come to Tuvalu.

And then, earlier this week, that already modest number was whittled down further to just two: Mauritius and Timor Leste, which together contribute to perhaps 0.01 or 0.02 per cent of global emissions.
Mr Bowen was even denying that the government had promised to bring "world leaders" to Tuvalu at all on Wednesday morning.
"No, I said we wanted to bring the world to Tuvalu," he said.
"We said we wanted to focus and lift the world's attention on the issues of the Pacific, small island developing states in particular, and I think it ticked that box and achieved that."
To call this cute is being generous.

If the minister is seriously trying to suggest that he did not mean "world leaders" when he said he wanted to bring "the world" to a "special leaders event" in the Pacific, then he is pushing credulity beyond breaking point.

It would also be a revelation to Australian officials who spent months (before the inevitable backdown) telling foreign officials that Australia and the Pacific were absolutely set on leaders only meeting in Tuvalu, and who were adamant ministerial level representation would not be contemplated.
Can promises turn into cash for Pacific nations?
It is possible to feel a twinge of sympathy here.
One Australia government source, frustrated by the "relentless negativity" around pre-COP, complained a few weeks ago that they were caught in a bit of a bind.
"If we push for leaders we get hammered for being unrealistic," they told the ABC.
"And if we don't (get leaders) then we get hammered for f***ing it up."
Fair enough.
But surely it would be better for the government to simply admit that it tried its best and fell short rather than blindly insisting everything is just dandy.
It is also worth pointing out that it might take a bit of time before anyone can truly say whether this pre-COP was a proper flop, or merely a tad underwhelming.

The Australian government has spruiked the gathering as a priceless opportunity to extract more cash for the Pacific Resilience Facility — a new climate fund which has been set up to give Pacific nations much more rapid (and easier) access to desperately needed climate finance.
So far, the new contributions unveiled in Nadi have been — to put it gently — modest.

But Pacific officials have taken every opportunity in Fiji to push for more hefty contributions, and are clearly hoping to see those promises delivered as hard cash commitments at the main COP gathering next month in Türkiye.
None of this means that the pre-COP failures are a millstone which will be hung forever around this government's neck.
If you are in the Pacific, you are — infuriatingly — already well accustomed to being at the mercy of the decisions taken by much larger emitters, and the major fossil fuel exporters.
Pacific's battle at the heart of global negotiations
It is also worth noting that while the Australian government will have to wear some embarrassment, its diplomatic stocks in the Pacific have not seemed to suffer.

That really does matter at a time when Australia remains locked in a "permanent contest" in the region with China — which is both the world's largest single polluter and the engine room of the global clean energy revolution.

Multiple Pacific leaders and officials have made it clear that they were still glad to see the Pacific's battle with climate change put, once again, at the heart of global climate negotiations, whatever pre-COP's shortfalls.
As one Pacific official put it yesterday to the ABC: why should Australia be blamed for trying, just because other leaders could not be bothered showing up?

Even Vanuatu's Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu, who is not shy of criticising Australia on climate policies, made it clear that he did not blame the Albanese government for the underwhelming turnout.
"We were hoping for more (leaders)," he told Reuters.
"It just reflects the lack of attention and priority given to what Pacific nations consider the greatest threat to their future."
Chris Bowen and Anthony Albanese might be in the cross hairs right now, but if pre-COP (and COP) fall hopelessly short once again, then there will be plenty of blame to go around.
